overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Disqualified Fuels to the Origin of Chanukah
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 21a–21b
overview.hebrewSource: בְּכ״ה בְּכִסְלֵיו יוֹמֵי דַחֲנוּכָּה תְּמָנְיָא אִינּוּן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing the mishna's list of disqualified oils and wicks, the Gemara clarifies that all of them remain fine for warmth or a bonfire — only their use as a wick for a lamp is restricted. It identifies kik oil, explains Rabba's two underlying reasons (poor wicks flicker; poor oils aren't drawn upward), and works through whether one may mix a good oil into a bad one to render it usable. That leads to a Temple-oil standard, and then — triggered by whether Shabbat-disqualified materials may fuel a Chanukah lamp — the daf turns fully to the halakhot of Chanukah: how many lights the mehadrin min hamehadrin light each night, where the lamp is placed, and the Gemara's own telling of the miracle of the single flask of oil.

slides.title: 🛢️ Disqualified as a Wick, Fine for a Bonfire
slides.text: A Tosefta clarifies the scope of the mishna's ban: all the materials disqualified for the Shabbat lamp's wick may still be piled into a bonfire — for warmth or for light, on the ground or on a stove. The Sages only prohibited making a wick from them. Along the way, the Gemara identifies שֶׁמֶן קִיק (kik oil): Shmuel heard from seafarers it comes from a coastal bird; Reish Lakish says it is oil from the plant of Jonah, which Rabba bar bar Chana describes seeing — like a ricinus tree, grown for shade over shop entrances, its seeds pressed for oil.
slides.hebrewSource: כׇּל אֵלּוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ אֵין מַדְלִיקִין בָּהֶן בְּשַׁבָּת, אֲבָל עוֹשִׂין מֵהֶן מְדוּרָה

slides.title: 🥜 Can a Bad Oil Be 'Fixed' by Mixing In a Good One?
slides.subtitle: Abaye presses Rabba on whether a small addition of kosher oil helps

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: May one add any amount of a permitted oil into a disqualified oil, and then light the mixture?

lines.speaker: Rabba
lines.text: One may not light it. Why? Because — one may not light it. (No further reason is given.)

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: But a Tosefta says: if you wrap a permitted wick around a nut and light it — Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that was his father's very custom!

lines.speaker: Rabba
lines.text: That case is about floating the wick on the oil using the nut, not combining materials to burn together.

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: But Rav Beruna cited Rav: melted forbidden fat or dissolved fish innards may have any amount of good oil added, and then be lit!

lines.speaker: Resolution
lines.text: Those are drawn by the wick even in their natural state; ordinary disqualified oils are not. And the Sages won't add a decree on top of a decree.

callout.label: Net result:
callout.text: Ordinary disqualified wicks and oils can't be salvaged by dilution — but fat or fish oil that already burns reasonably well may be boosted with any amount of good oil.

slides.title: 🕎 Using Shabbat-Disqualified Materials for the Chanukah Lamp
slides.subtitle: Three amoraic positions, turning on what happens if the light goes out
rows: Forbidden on Chanukah too, weekday or Shabbat — must burn reliably from the start
No — but light may still be used
Permitted on weekdays; forbidden on Shabbat, lest one adjust the wick
No relighting required, and its light may not be used
Permitted even on Shabbat — no concern about adjusting, since using the light is forbidden anyway

callout.label: How halakha settled:
callout.text: Abaye at first didn't accept this ruling in Rabbi Yirmeya's name, but accepted the identical ruling once it came in Rabbi Yochanan's name — later admitting he wished he had learned it from the start, since knowledge from one's youth is retained best.

slides.title: 8️⃣ Beit Shammai vs. Beit Hillel on the Nightly Count
slides.subtitle: The mehadrin min hamehadrin — the most scrupulous practice

boxes.title: Beit Shammai: Count Down
items: Light eight on night one, decreasing to one
Reason A: corresponds to the incoming days of Chanukah still ahead
Reason B: corresponds to the bulls offered on Sukkot, which decrease day by day

boxes.title: Beit Hillel: Count Up
items: Light one on night one, increasing to eight
Reason A: corresponds to the outgoing days already completed
Reason B: 'one elevates in sanctity, never lowers' — the accepted halakha

callout.label: Real people, real practice:
callout.text: Rabbi Yochanan reports two Elders in Sidon who each followed a different house, each explaining his own practice with one of the two reasons above.

slides.title: ✨ Why We Light: The Chanukah Story
slides.subtitle: Placement rules and the miracle itself, from Megillat Taanit

nodes.content: 🏛️ Mitzva: place the lamp at the entrance outside; upstairs, at the window facing the public domain; in danger, on the table
🕯️ Rava: one needs a separate light to use for its light — unless there's a bonfire, or unless one is an 'important person' who still needs a separate light
⚔️ When the Greeks entered the Sanctuary, they defiled all the oil in it
🏺 When the Hasmoneans defeated them, they searched and found only one flask of pure oil — sealed by the High Priest — enough for one day
🎉 A miracle occurred and it burned eight days; the next year the Sages fixed these days as a holiday of Hallel and thanksgiving

callout.label: Same daf, closing note:
callout.text: A mishna on damages is then cited to introduce the next sugya: liability when a spark, or a camel's flax passing a storekeeper's lamp, causes a fire.

summary.principle: Materials disqualified as a Shabbat wick remain usable for warmth or a bonfire, and that same care over reliable, undiminished light carries directly into the halakhot of the Chanukah lamp — climaxing in the Gemara's account of the miracle it commemorates.

8️⃣ Beit Shammai counts down, Beit Hillel counts up — halakha follows Beit Hillel

flowSteps.content: ✨ The story: one day's oil burns for eight, commemorated with Hallel and thanksgiving
🎓 Key Principle: reliability and full brightness of the light — never merely partial or borrowed fuel — is the throughline from Shabbat's lamp to Chanukah's

quiz.q: According to the Tosefta, what is permitted with oils and wicks that are disqualified for the Shabbat lamp?
o: Nothing — they may not be used at all on Shabbat
They may still be used to build a bonfire for warmth or light
They may only be used by a gentile
They may be used only in the Temple
quiz.e: The Tosefta states that the Sages only prohibited making a wick from these materials; they remain permitted for a bonfire, whether for warmth or for its light.

quiz.q: Why does Rabba rule that one may not light a mixture of a disqualified oil with any amount of a permitted oil added?
o: Because mixing oils is always forbidden by Torah law
Because it remains governed by the basic rule that one may not light with disqualified oil
Because mixtures are muktzeh
Because only pure olive oil may ever be used
quiz.e: Rabba's terse answer is that the reason is simply that one may not light with it — the underlying concern being that people might come to light the disqualified oil in its natural, undiluted form.

quiz.q: According to Rav Chisda's position on using Shabbat-disqualified wicks and oils for the Chanukah lamp, what is the ruling?
o: Permitted on weekdays but forbidden on Shabbat, since one might adjust the wick to keep it lit for using its light
Forbidden always, weekday and Shabbat alike
Permitted always, weekday and Shabbat alike
Permitted only in the Temple
quiz.e: Rav Chisda holds that if the Chanukah light goes out one need not relight it, but since its light may be used, one must ensure on Shabbat itself that it burns well — hence disqualified materials are forbidden specifically on Shabbat.

quiz.q: What is the halakha regarding the mehadrin min hamehadrin practice of increasing or decreasing Chanukah lights each night?
o: Beit Shammai's view is accepted: decrease from eight to one
Beit Hillel's view is accepted: increase from one to eight, based on 'one elevates in sanctity and does not lower'
Both views are accepted depending on location
Neither view is followed; one light is lit every night
quiz.e: The accepted halakha follows Beit Hillel: light one lamp on the first night and increase by one each subsequent night, reflecting the principle that sanctity is increased, never decreased.

quiz.q: According to the account in the Gemara, how long was the found flask of oil originally sufficient to last, and what happened?
o: Eight days originally; nothing miraculous occurred
One day; a miracle caused it to burn for eight days
It never ran out at all
Three days; it lasted exactly three
quiz.e: The Gemara relates that the flask found with the seal of the High Priest held enough oil for only one day's lighting, but a miracle occurred and it burned for eight days, which the Sages then established as the holiday of Chanukah.
